blocks.text: An increase in temperature increases the reaction rate: the rate doubles or triples for every 10 degrees C rise. Temperature usually has a major effect, because molecules at higher temperature have more thermal energy and so collide more frequently and with greater energy. The Boltzmann distribution curve shows the distribution of molecular energies at a certain temperature: a few particles have very low energy, a few very high energy, and many have energies in between. The area under the curve represents the number of particles, and the shaded area beyond the activation energy Ea represents the proportion of molecules with enough energy to cause a chemical change when they collide.

As the temperature of a reaction mixture is raised, the average kinetic energy of the particles increases; they move more quickly, collide more frequently, and the proportion of successful collisions rises greatly. The Boltzmann curve at the higher temperature flattens and its peak shifts to the right, and for a 10 degrees C rise the shaded area beyond Ea approximately doubles. In conclusion, raising the temperature increases the rate of a reaction.

blocks.alt: Left: two humped curves of number of molecules against energy, a tall blue one for the lower temperature and a flatter red one shifted right for the higher, with a dashed vertical line at Ea and the areas beyond it shaded. Right: an energy path with a high red hump for the uncatalysed reaction and a lower green hump for the catalysed one, both from the same reactant level to the same product level.
blocks.caption: The Boltzmann distribution at two temperatures and the energy path of a catalysed and an uncatalysed reaction (original diagram after Figures 7.6 to 7.8; curves schematic).
blocks.long_description: The area under each curve is the total number of molecules and the shaded tail beyond Ea is the fraction able to react. At the higher temperature the peak moves right and the curve flattens, so the tail roughly doubles for a 10 degree rise, and the molecules also collide more often: the rate rises sharply. A catalyst does not change the reactants, products or delta H; it opens a new path over a lower barrier, so a larger share of the molecules already present can cross it.

blocks.prompt: What is the Boltzmann distribution curve, and why does a 10 degrees C rise roughly double the rate?
blocks.explanation: It is the graph of the number of molecules against their energy at a given temperature, a hump with a long tail of high energies; the area under it is the number of molecules and the tail beyond Ea the number able to react. Warming by 10 degrees shifts the curve right and flattens it, which roughly doubles the area beyond Ea, so about twice as many collisions are effective and the rate roughly doubles.

items: Rate roughly doubles or triples per 10 degrees C rise: molecules move faster, collide more often and with more energy.
Boltzmann distribution: number of molecules against energy; the area beyond Ea is the reacting fraction, and it roughly doubles for a 10 degree rise as the peak shifts right and the curve flattens.
